description: Why 22 Minutes? Because a signal traveling between Mars and Earth can take approximately 22 mins to arrive. While a signal takes millions of kilometers to reach Earth, we believe great ideas can travel even further — turning scientific discoveries into meaningful solutions for humanity. Because even the smallest signal can inspire the biggest change. 🌍
summary:
We are Team 22 Minutes, people of the Caspian. We grew up on its shores, as generations of our ancestors did before us. This is our Khazar—a sea whose shores saw one of the world's first mechanically drilled oil wells in 1846.
Today, the Caspian is changing. Falling water levels, retreating shorelines, shrinking wetlands, threats to biodiversity, and exposed seabeds that may contribute to dust pollution put coastal ecosystems and communities at risk.
We created Caspian Pulse, an interactive dashboard designed to use NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations to track coastal change across one location as demo, highlight meaningful signals, and help relevant agencies identify where closer investigation and action may be needed.
We also developed a prototype game with four characters, introducing children to environmental challenges informed by our findings and showing how informed choices can make a difference.
Our project is born on the Caspian, designed for the world: Caspian Pulse could be adapted to help communities monitor vulnerable coastlines anywhere.
Because every coastline has a pulse. We just need to listen.
details:
Our planet faces numerous environmental challenges, and coastal regions are increasingly vulnerable to changing water levels, erosion, and ecosystem degradation.

We are Team 22 Minutes, a group of young innovators who grew up on the shores of the Caspian Sea. Inspired by our connection to Khazar and concerned about its declining water levels, retreating shorelines, and threatened biodiversity, we created Caspian Pulse.

Caspian Pulse is an interactive platform that combines satellite-based environmental observation with educational gaming.

Our project has two main components:

  • Pulse Observatory: A scientific exploration dashboard using NASA–ISRO NISAR radar data and supporting NASA Earth observation imagery. Our prototype focuses on the Baku–Absheron coastal region, with three date-pair comparisons and 33 image-based investigation areas. It helps users explore satellite observations and identify signals that may warrant further investigation.
  • Guardians of the Earth: An interactive educational game featuring four characters — Botanist, Engineer, Data Scientist, and Climate Scout. Players investigate environmental signals, analyze clues, and make decisions through simulated challenges inspired by real satellite imagery.

Our mission is to make Earth observation data more accessible, raise environmental awareness among younger generations, and demonstrate how satellite technology can support evidence-informed coastal monitoring.

Starting with our home, we envision expanding Caspian Pulse to other vulnerable coastal regions worldwide, connecting science, education, and environmental responsibility.
